title: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)
subtitle: The reliable, ordered byte stream that most of the Internet is built on.
summary: TCP gives two programs a reliable, in-order stream of bytes over an unreliable network that only delivers individual packets. It numbers every byte, acknowledges what arrives, retransmits what does not, and sets up and tears down each connection with a defined exchange of control segments. RFC 9293 is the consolidated specification that replaces RFC 793 and folds in forty years of fixes.

plainLanguage.summary: TCP gives two programs a reliable, in-order stream of bytes over a network that delivers only individual packets. It numbers every byte, acknowledges what arrives, retransmits what does not, and opens and closes each connection with a defined exchange of control segments. RFC 9293 is the consolidated specification that replaces RFC 793 and includes forty years of fixes.

tldr.problem: The Internet only delivers individual packets, which can be lost, duplicated, delayed or reordered, but applications want a dependable stream.
tldr.mechanism: TCP numbers every byte, acknowledges received data cumulatively, retransmits on timeout, limits the sender with a receive window and congestion control, and uses SYN and FIN exchanges to open and close connections.
tldr.outcome: Web pages, email, file transfers and many other applications can treat the network as a pipe that delivers bytes in order, and RFC 9293 is now the single document that defines how.

today: TCP carries the bulk of traffic for the web (HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2), email, SSH and many other applications, and TLS is normally layered on top of it. Every mainstream operating system ships a TCP stack, and packet analyzers such as Wireshark and tcpdump decode the header described here. Newer transports such as QUIC were designed in part from lessons learned with TCP, but TCP remains the default choice for a reliable stream.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 793, published in 1981, defined TCP. For decades it was the core specification, but fixes and improvements piled up in many other documents, and numerous errata were filed against it. RFC 9293 gathers the Standards Track changes and clarifications into one updated specification and obsoletes RFC 793, so a new implementer no longer has to piece the protocol together from a dozen RFCs.

The document describes the common basis every TCP implementation must support in order to interoperate. It deliberately points to companion documents for large topics such as congestion control and the high-performance extensions instead of reproducing them, and it labels each requirement (MUST-1, SHLD-5 and so on) so conformance can be checked.

RFC 9293 states the service plainly: TCP provides a reliable, in-order, byte-stream service to applications, carried in IP datagrams, between exactly two endpoints (unicast).
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 793 (1981) defined TCP, but fixes accumulated in many other documents. RFC 9293 gathers the Standards Track changes into one specification and obsoletes RFC 793. It describes what every TCP implementation must support to interoperate, and points to companion documents for topics such as congestion control. TCP gives a reliable, in-order byte-stream service between exactly two endpoints.

sections.title: Byte Stream and Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
Applications hand TCP a stream of bytes, and TCP chops it into segments, each sent as one IP datagram. Every byte of data has its own sequence number, so every byte can be acknowledged. Acknowledgments are cumulative: an acknowledgment number X means all bytes up to but not including X have arrived.

The sequence space is 32 bits (0 to 232 - 1), and all arithmetic on it is done modulo 232. The SYN and FIN flags each occupy one sequence number, but a bare ACK occupies none, which avoids acknowledging acknowledgments.

A new connection does not start counting at zero. It picks an initial sequence number (ISN) from a 32-bit clock that ticks roughly every 4 microseconds, so old segments from an earlier use of the same address and port pair are unlikely to be mistaken for new ones. RFC 9293 also folds in the more secure ISN generation from RFC 6528, because predictable ISNs let an off-path attacker forge segments.

Segments from an earlier incarnation of a connection are further kept at bay by the TIME-WAIT state and, in principle, by a "quiet time" of one maximum segment lifetime (taken to be 2 minutes) after a host loses its sequence-number memory.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP splits an application's byte stream into segments, each sent in one IP datagram. Every byte has a sequence number, and acknowledgments are cumulative: acknowledgment number X means all bytes before X have arrived. A new connection starts at an initial sequence number taken from a 32-bit clock, so old segments are unlikely to be mistaken for new ones. The secure generation from RFC 6528 is included.

sections.title: The TCP Header
sections.content:
Every segment starts with a header of at least 20 bytes (five 32-bit words). It carries 16-bit source and destination port numbers, which identify the application services and let many conversations share a pair of hosts, followed by the 32-bit sequence and acknowledgment numbers.

The 4-bit Data Offset counts the header length in 32-bit words, so it tells the receiver where the data begins. Next come 4 reserved bits and eight single-bit flags: CWR, ECE, URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN and FIN. The 16-bit Window says how many bytes the sender of the segment is willing to accept, and the 16-bit Checksum covers the header, the data and a pseudo-header borrowed from the IP layer. The checksum is never optional: the sender MUST generate it and the receiver MUST check it.

Options follow the fixed fields. Every implementation MUST support three: End of Option List (kind 0), No-Operation (kind 1) and Maximum Segment Size (kind 2, length 4). Options other than kinds 0 and 1 carry a length field, so unknown ones can be skipped.
sections.plainLanguage: Every segment starts with a header of at least 20 bytes. It holds 16-bit source and destination port numbers, the 32-bit sequence and acknowledgment numbers, a data offset showing where the data begins, eight flag bits (such as SYN, ACK, FIN and RST), a window size and a checksum. The checksum is never optional. Options follow the fixed fields, and unknown options can be skipped.

sections.title: Opening a Connection
sections.content:
A connection is opened with the three-way handshake. The side that opens actively sends a SYN carrying its initial sequence number. The other side, which was waiting in LISTEN after a passive open, replies with a SYN that also acknowledges the first one (SYN,ACK). The first side then sends an ACK, and both are ESTABLISHED. In RFC 9293's example the first peer starts at sequence 100 and the second at 300, so the acknowledgments say 101 and 301.

The handshake exists mainly to keep old duplicate SYNs from creating false connections. If a stale SYN arrives, the reply carries an acknowledgment the original sender does not expect, and it answers with a RST (reset) so the confused side goes back to LISTEN. Two peers can also open at the same moment (simultaneous open), and an implementation MUST support that.

Data may ride along with the handshake, but the receiver must not hand it to the application until the connection is ESTABLISHED.
sections.plainLanguage: A connection opens with a three-way handshake. The opener sends a SYN with its initial sequence number. The other side replies with a SYN that also acknowledges the first (SYN,ACK), and the opener sends an ACK. Both are then ESTABLISHED. This mainly stops old duplicate SYNs from creating false connections; a stale one draws a RST (reset). Simultaneous open must also work.

sections.title: States and Closing a Connection
sections.content:
Each connection is in one of eleven states: LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT-1, FIN-WAIT-2, CLOSE-WAIT, CLOSING, LAST-ACK, TIME-WAIT, and the fictional CLOSED, which means no connection record exists. State changes are driven by user calls (OPEN, SEND, RECEIVE, CLOSE, ABORT, STATUS), incoming segments with SYN, ACK, RST or FIN set, and timeouts.

CLOSE means only "I have no more data to send." Each direction is closed separately with a FIN, so a connection can be half-closed: one side finished sending but still receives. In the normal close, the side that closes first goes through FIN-WAIT-1 and FIN-WAIT-2 and finally TIME-WAIT, where it waits 2 MSL before deleting the connection. The wait ensures the last ACK was received and lets stray delayed segments die out. An abrupt end is a reset: one or more RST segments are sent and the state is discarded.

The state diagram in the RFC is explicitly a summary, not the whole specification. Its notes add that a RST can be sent from any state, and that FIN-WAIT-1 can go directly to TIME-WAIT when a FIN arrives together with the ACK of the local FIN.
sections.plainLanguage: Each connection is in one of eleven states, such as LISTEN, ESTABLISHED and TIME-WAIT. CLOSE means only "I have no more data to send." Each direction closes separately with a FIN, so a connection can be half-closed. The side that closes first ends in TIME-WAIT, waiting 2 MSL (twice the maximum segment lifetime) so stray delayed segments die out. An abrupt end uses RST.

sections.title: Segmentation, Windows and Reliability
sections.content:
The Maximum Segment Size option, sent in a SYN, tells the peer the largest segment payload it can receive. If none arrives, TCP MUST assume 536 bytes for IPv4 or 1220 for IPv6. The size actually sent is the smaller of the peer's limit and what the local IP layer allows, minus header sizes.

The 16-bit window in each segment limits how much unacknowledged data the sender may have in flight, so a slow receiver is not overrun. Implementations are advised to keep window values in 32-bit variables. Window scaling and the other high-performance extensions are in RFC 7323 and are not described in RFC 9293.

Lost data is repaired by retransmission. The retransmission timeout is computed as in RFC 6298 (including Karn's algorithm), and an endpoint MUST implement slow start, congestion avoidance and exponential backoff of the timeout (see RFC 5681) to avoid congestion collapse. ECN (RFC 3168) is a SHOULD. A sender SHOULD apply the Nagle algorithm (RFC 896) to coalesce small writes, but applications MUST be able to turn it off per connection.

Keep-alives are optional; if present they MUST default to off, with an interval of no less than two hours. The urgent mechanism MUST be implemented, but new applications SHOULD NOT use it.
sections.plainLanguage: The Maximum Segment Size option in a SYN tells the peer the largest segment it can receive; the default is 536 bytes for IPv4 and 1220 for IPv6. The window in each segment limits unacknowledged data in flight, so a slow receiver is not overrun. Lost data is retransmitted, and implementations must use slow start, congestion avoidance and exponential backoff of the retransmission timeout to avoid congestion collapse.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
TCP has only rudimentary built-in protection: sequence numbers and checks that make connections robust, but no cryptography. Confidentiality and authentication come from other layers: IPsec, TLS above TCP, or the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO, RFC 5925). TCP-MD5 is described as flawed and deprecated. TLS protects the data but not the TCP header.

RFC 9293 names several attack families. Off-path attackers who can guess ISNs or blind-inject segments, which is why RFC 6528 ISN generation and mitigations from RFC 5961 were incorporated. Resource exhaustion such as SYN flooding. ICMP-based attacks (see RFC 5927). Abuse of congestion control such as ACK-division. The text also notes that TCP's cleartext header exposes metadata to anyone on the path (its "wire image", RFC 8546), and that stack behavior can be used to fingerprint the operating system.

Do not treat TCP itself as a secure channel. Anything sent over plain TCP can be read, and its control flags can be forged, by an on-path attacker.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP has no cryptography. Its sequence numbers and checks make connections robust but do not provide secrecy or authentication. Those come from IPsec, TLS or the TCP Authentication Option (RFC 5925). Listed attacks include off-path guessing of sequence numbers, SYN flooding and ICMP-based attacks. Its cleartext header exposes metadata to anyone on the path. Plain TCP can be read and its flags forged by an on-path attacker.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 793
sections.content:
RFC 9293 is mostly an editorial consolidation, adapted from the functional specification in section 3 of RFC 793. Accepted errata were incorporated, and the normative parts of several documents were folded in: the urgent-pointer clarifications from RFC 1011, RFC 1122 and RFC 6093, the secure ISN algorithm from RFC 6528, the RTO text now pointing to RFC 6298, the resource-reclaiming clarification from RFC 6429, and a description of congestion control based on current Standards Track documents.

The index lists RFC 9293 as obsoleting RFC 793, RFC 879, RFC 2873, RFC 6093, RFC 6429, RFC 6528 and RFC 6691. It does not obsolete RFC 1122, which covers more than TCP; it only updates it, though the RFC says it effectively replaces RFC 1122's TCP material. Informational background in the older documents remains valuable.

RFC 7414, the TCP roadmap, remains the guide to the surrounding family of enhancement RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 9293 is mostly an editorial consolidation of the functional specification in RFC 793. It incorporates accepted errata, the urgent-pointer clarifications, the secure initial sequence number algorithm from RFC 6528, and a description of congestion control based on current Standards Track documents. It obsoletes RFC 793 and several other RFCs, but only updates RFC 1122.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Sequence number of the first data octet; if SYN is set, the initial sequence number.

fields.name: Acknowledgment Number
fields.desc: If ACK is set, the next sequence number the sender expects to receive.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Must be zero when sent and ignored when received.

fields.name: Window
fields.desc: Number of data octets the sender is willing to accept, starting at the acknowledgment number.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Ones' complement checksum over the header, data and pseudo-header; never optional.

fields.name: Urgent Pointer
fields.desc: Offset to the octet following the urgent data; meaningful only with URG.

fields.name: Options (variable)
fields.desc: Present only when Data Offset is greater than 5; a multiple of 32 bits including padding. Shown here as one word.

messages.label: SYN  SEQ=100
messages.note: A: CLOSED to SYN-SENT. B: LISTEN to SYN-RECEIVED.

messages.label: SYN,ACK  SEQ=300 ACK=101
messages.note: Acknowledges the SYN, which used sequence number 100. A becomes ESTABLISHED.

messages.label: ACK + data  SEQ=101 ACK=301
messages.note: The sequence number is unchanged because a bare ACK uses no sequence space.

transitions.label: rcv RST (only if reached by passive OPEN)
rcv FIN with ACK of FIN (note 2)

messages.label: FIN,ACK  SEQ=100 ACK=300
messages.note: A closes: ESTABLISHED to FIN-WAIT-1. B moves to CLOSE-WAIT.

messages.label: ACK  SEQ=300 ACK=101
messages.note: A moves to FIN-WAIT-2. B may keep sending until its user closes.

messages.label: FIN,ACK  SEQ=300 ACK=101
messages.note: B's user closes: B moves to LAST-ACK. A moves to TIME-WAIT.

messages.label: ACK  SEQ=101 ACK=301
messages.note: B becomes CLOSED. A waits 2 MSL, then becomes CLOSED.

items.title: Sequence numbers and ACKs
items.text: Every byte is numbered; cumulative acknowledgments show what has arrived and expose duplicates.

items.title: Checksum
items.text: A mandatory 16-bit checksum over header, data and a pseudo-header detects corruption and misrouted segments.

items.title: Retransmission
items.text: The sender keeps unacknowledged data and resends it when a dynamically computed timeout expires (RFC 6298).

items.title: Flow and congestion control
items.text: The advertised window protects the receiver; slow start, congestion avoidance and backoff protect the network.

data.title: Effective send MSS
data.code:
Eff.snd.MSS = min(SendMSS + 20, MMS_S) - TCPhdrsize - IPoptionsize

SendMSS      MSS received from the peer, or the default
             536 (IPv4) / 1220 (IPv6) if no MSS option arrived
MMS_S        largest transport-layer message TCP may send
TCPhdrsize   20 plus any TCP options being sent
IPoptionsize IPv4 options or IPv6 extension headers in use
